title: Is the Ramsey number R(5,5) equal to 43?
credit: Conjecture R(5,5)=43: B. McKay and S. Radziszowski (1997); bounds: Exoo (1989), Angeltveit-McKay (2018, 2024).
premise_risks: Board already has R(3,10) and R(3,3,3,3); owner may consider a third exact Ramsey value too similar in style, though R(5,5) is the canonical diagonal case
Primarily computational; a proof would likely be computer-assisted and hard to formalise as a Lean proof (statement itself is trivial to formalise)
plain: R(5,5) is the least n such that every graph on n vertices contains either 5 mutually adjacent vertices or 5 mutually non-adjacent vertices. Exoo's 1989 graph on 42 vertices has neither, so R(5,5) >= 43; computer-assisted work of Angeltveit and McKay (2024) gives R(5,5) <= 46. Determine R(5,5); the expected answer is 43, i.e. every graph on 43 vertices has a clique or an independent set of size 5.
math: Determine $R(5,5)$, where $R(5,5)=\min\{n:\ \forall G \text{ on } n \text{ vertices},\ \omega(G)\ge5 \text{ or } \alpha(G)\ge5\}$. Known: $43\le R(5,5)\le 46$. Board claim: $R(5,5)=43$, i.e. every simple graph $G$ on $43$ vertices has $\omega(G)\ge5$ or $\alpha(G)\ge5$. (Determining the value exactly, whichever of 43--46 it is, also resolves the problem; an upper bound $\le 45$ is partial progress.)
